title: Clutter, colour and accessibility
summary: Delete everything that doesn’t help the message, label directly, use one accent colour against grey, choose colours everyone can tell apart, and add alt text.
objectives: Remove chart junk: legends for one series, heavy gridlines, borders, 3-D and spare decimals.
Label series and values directly instead of making readers match colours to a legend.
Use one accent colour for the point and grey for the rest.
Choose colour-blind-safe colours and write alt text.

p: Everything on a chart either helps the message or gets in its way. Excel’s defaults add a lot that gets in the way.
Before: a legend for one series, a label on every column, gridlines, a border, and “Chart Title”.
After: one line, a finding title, nothing to decode.
Ask of every element: would the reader miss it if it went?
In real life: is “no element without a job”. The monthly pack shrank from 22 pages to 9, and the regional heads started reading it.

p: Most clutter falls into a few types. Delete them, or make them lighter.
Labels **or** an axis with gridlines: rarely both.
Keep axis lines light grey, not black.
Never use 3-D: the front of a 3-D bar sits higher than its value.
In real life: redrew its branch dashboard without 3-D. Two branches that looked equal had a 9% gap: the 3-D perspective had hidden it.

p: A legend makes readers look away, match a colour, and look back. Put the name **at the end of the line** instead.
In Excel: click the last point of a line › **Add Data Label**, then show the **Series Name**.
With labels on, delete the legend.
For pies, label each slice with its name and %.
In real life: banned legends on line charts. Readers spend their few seconds on the data, not on matching colours.

check.q: A column chart of one series has a legend, gridlines and a label on every column. What should go?
options: The legend, and either the gridlines or the labels
check.explain: One series needs no legend. Labels and gridlines do the same job: keep one.

why.0: Each of those is doing a job already done elsewhere.
why.2: The title should stay, saying the finding.

slides.h: One accent colour, the rest grey
p: Colour is the strongest signal on a chart. Use **one accent colour** for what matters and **grey** for everything else.
The eye goes straight to the coloured bar.
Red–green for bad–good fails for many readers; use a blue accent with words.
Same colour, same meaning: if East is blue on one chart, keep it blue on the next.
In real life: used five colours for five regions. The CEO asked, “What am I supposed to look at?” The next version had one blue column: East.

spec.title: East grew slowest: 4.8%, half South’s pace

p: About **1 in 12 men** and 1 in 200 women have a colour vision deficiency, most often red–green. Pick colours that stay distinct for them.
Blue with orange, and dark with light, stay distinct for almost everyone.
Don’t use colour as the only clue: add labels or words.
Check: **Review › Check Accessibility** flags some problems; printing in greyscale shows the rest.
In real life: used red for fail and green for pass. A parent who is colour-blind couldn’t tell which subjects his son had failed.

p: Make the chart readable by everyone: a finding title, alt text for screen readers, and text big and dark enough to read.
Alt text: right-click the chart › **Edit Alt Text** (**View Alt Text** in some versions).
Good alt text: “Column chart of growth by region. South grew most, 10%; East slowest, 4.8%.”
Bad alt text: “Chart 3”.
In real life: must publish accessible reports. Their analysts write the alt text as they make each chart: it takes a minute, and it improves the title too.

tasks.prompt: You need two colours that almost everyone can tell apart. Which pair?

That pair is red and green.

real.title: Clean up a chart in Excel
steps: Download **Tulsi Mart growth chart**. The **Regions** sheet has growth by region and a chart someone made in a hurry: legend, gridlines, no labels, and a topic for a title.
Select the chart and click **+** (Chart Elements; on a Mac, **Chart Design › Add Chart Element**). **Untick Legend and Gridlines**, and **tick Data Labels**.
Grey first: click any column **once** (that selects them all), then right-click › **Format Data Series › Fill › Solid fill** and pick a light grey.
Now make **East** stand out: click the East column **twice**, slowly (the second click selects just that one), then **Format Data Point › Fill › Solid fill** in a strong blue.
Click the title and replace it with the **finding about East**: for example, East grew slowest: 4.8%, half South’s pace.
Right-click the chart › **Edit Alt Text** (or **View Alt Text**) and describe it in a sentence or two: the chart type, what it shows, and the finding.
Save as .xlsx and upload it here.

points: Delete **chart junk**: one-series legends, heavy gridlines, borders, 3-D, spare decimals.
**Label directly** and use **one accent colour**, the rest grey.
Use **colour-blind-safe** colours, never colour alone, and add **alt text**.
